title: Game Studio
tagline: Your game. Your rules. Real quality control.
objectives: I can use if/else so my game reacts differently to different situations.
I can personalise a game while still meeting a design brief's required features.
I can test my own game against a checklist before showing it to others.

config.headline: You fixed their game. Now ship your own.
lines: In this lesson you will learn the block that lets a game make a DECISION: **if/else**. The game asks one question, like: is the apple touching the bowl? Then it runs exactly one of two sets of blocks — one set if the answer is yes, a different set if the answer is no. Computing calls this **SELECTION**, and it is the difference between a slideshow and a game.

Last lesson your QA team rescued Shark Attack. Today OLS GAMES is hiring new studios — and one of them is yours. Three **CONTRACTS** are on the desk — a contract is a signed deal to build one game. Yours will be a catching game, a maze escape, or a quiz show. Every contract demands the SAME three things — your game must **choose**, **count**, and **end** — but everything else is yours: your name, your look, your rules.

One more thing. Tonight is **PRESS NIGHT**: the class plays the game you ship, and your studio gets its first signed reviews. Every game gets played by real players — so every studio tests its own game hard before the doors open.
Today you hold both jobs: designer and QA tester. Time to open your doors.
config.help: This screen is only for reading — it tells you what today's lesson is about. When the writing finishes, press the button at the bottom to start.

config.title: Three contracts on the desk
config.intro: Read all three contracts before you sign — you are choosing the game you will ship tonight. There is no easy option: every contract carries the same BRIEF (the list of things your game must do), the same checks and the same XP. When you sign, you sign with a STUDIO NAME — pick one you will be proud for the whole class to see tonight.
config.introSolo: Catch-up day — the studios have been and gone, but the contracts are still on the desk. Read all three, pick the game you will build, and sign with a STUDIO NAME you would be proud of. Every contract carries the same BRIEF (the list of things your game must do), the same checks and the same XP, whichever you choose.
config.signNote: Signed the wrong one? You can tear a contract up and re-sign — right up until your first QA test is recorded. (Re-signing means a fresh kit: anything you built in Scratch stays with the old contract.)

brief.title: Every contract carries the same brief
items: TRACK — a variable that changes in play
END — a game that can finish
WORKS — passes all four QA tests

contracts.name: Catch It
contracts.headline: The arcade classic
contracts.pitch: Apples fall, and one bowl waits below. Miss three and the game is over — if you build it that way.
contracts.imgAlt: The Catch It starter: an apple falling from a blue sky toward a bowl
ships: A bowl that moves on the arrow keys
An apple that falls, lands, and falls again
Sky, ground and sounds, ready to go
adds: Game over the instant lives hit zero
contracts.theme: Re-skin everything: catch sushi, stars, or falling socks — if it falls, it plays.

contracts.name: Maze Escape
contracts.headline: The escape room
contracts.pitch: The walls bounce you back to the start. Three stars glitter in the corners — and one locked door stands between your beetle and freedom.
contracts.imgAlt: The Maze Escape starter: a beetle in a walled maze with stars and a locked door
ships: A beetle with full arrow-key controls
Walls that already bounce you back to the start
Three stars that vanish when touched — but nothing counts them
A door that senses you arrive… and does nothing about it
adds: the stars counter, wired to all three stars
THE if/else at the door: earned your escape, or not?
A proper ending when the door swings open
contracts.theme: Re-skin it: haunted house, space station, the school at midnight.

contracts.name: Quiz Master
contracts.headline: The quiz show
contracts.pitch: Three questions, two answer tiles, and a host who never stops talking. It is the quickest quiz show on television — and you write the script.
contracts.imgAlt: The Quiz Master starter: a host by a chalkboard with T and F answer tiles
ships: A host who asks three questions in a row
T and F answer tiles that already sense every click
A question flow that runs itself
adds: the score, displayed on stage for the audience
THE if/else inside each tile: right… or wrong?
A finale that announces the final score
contracts.theme: The questions are YOURS: football, K-pop, Minecraft, Irish — you're the quizmaster now.

config.help: Read all three contracts, then press Sign on the one you WANT to build — same brief, same checks, same XP whichever you pick. Type a studio name you would be proud to see up in lights. You can tear it up and re-sign right up until your first QA test is recorded.

strings.tearArm: Click again to shred this contract

config.fallback: If the film won't load, don't worry — your teacher's demonstration covers everything it shows, and the cards on this screen walk you through the rest.
config.help: Watch the if/else chapter even if you picked Maze or Quiz — the block is exactly the same; your blueprint shows you where it goes in YOUR game. The worked example and the testing chapters wait on your Studio Desk, beside your blueprint, for the moment you need them.
config.note: The film builds ONE game — Catch It — because the if/else block is identical in all three contracts; your blueprint shows where it goes in YOURS. The worked example and the testing chapters live on your Studio Desk, right beside the blueprint.

config.intro: This is your SPRINT — one short, focused burst of building, about 25 minutes on the clock. Your desk has three zones. The KIT gets your game open in Scratch. The BLUEPRINT lists the exact blocks your contract needs. And four QA CHECKS stand between you and the gallery. You build your OWN game — the person beside you is your QA tester, and when your teacher calls the halfway swap, you run the four tests on each other's machines. Personalise everything you like, but remember what QA taught you last lesson: looking finished and working are two different things. The READY FOR GALLERY button only believes ticks.
config.introSolo: A solo sprint — one short burst of building, and you run your own tests today. Your desk has the same three zones: the kit, the blueprint, and the four QA checks. The same rule stands: the READY FOR GALLERY button only believes ticks.
config.pairNote: You each build your OWN game — but you're also your partner's QA tester. At the midpoint swap: run the four tests on THEIR machine while they run yours. A tester who didn't build it finds what the builder can't see.
config.qaIntro: Four checks stand between your build and the gallery. Run each test in Scratch, then record what ACTUALLY happened — not what you hoped. A cross isn't failure: it's QA doing its job, and it hands you the exact fix. When a check that failed turns green, it earns a FOUND BY QA tag — that is the desk doing its job, not a black mark.

kit.intro: Your starter kit is deliberately unfinished — it runs, but it cannot choose, count or end yet. Somewhere in its code sits a yellow STUDIO NOTE. A comment is a programmer's sticky-note — it does nothing when the game runs — and this one marks the exact spot where your big block will go. Get the kit open in Scratch:
kit.confirm: The kit is open in Scratch and I found the STUDIO NOTE comment in its code

marquee.title: Open the doors
marquee.intro: Your listing goes up on the class MARQUEE — the board of every studio's game, like film titles up in lights. It is how tonight's players choose where to play. Make yours worth a visit.
marquee.howPlaceholder: e.g. Arrow keys to move. Catch sushi, dodge the wasabi!
marquee.betaIntro: IN BETA is a real thing in real studios: showing a game that is not finished yet. Your listing goes up with an IN BETA tag, and players review what is there.

catch.name: Catch It
catch.noteWhere: Click the Apple in the sprite list — the STUDIO NOTE is stuck to its code, right beside the blocks that make the apple fall.

blueprint.title: The Catch It blueprint
blueprint.intro: Five moves, in order. The STUDIO NOTE comment in the Apple's code marks the exact spot for the big one.

steps.title: Make the variables
steps.text: Variables → Make a Variable → 'score'. Again → 'lives'. For all sprites, both times. New variables show on stage automatically — leave the ticks on.

steps.title: Set them at the flag
steps.text: On the Apple's when-flag script, before the forever loop: set score to 0, set lives to 3. Variables remember between games — without this, every new game inherits the old numbers.

steps.title: The if/else — the big one
steps.text: Control → if/else. It goes AFTER the fall loop, still INSIDE the forever (the STUDIO NOTE points at the spot). Condition: Sensing → touching Bowl?. Top mouth: change score by 1 + start sound pop. Bottom mouth (else): change lives by -1.

steps.title: The ending
steps.text: Inside the else, under 'change lives by -1': add an 'if' with Operators' (=) asking lives = 0. Inside it: say 'Game over!' for 2 seconds, then add 'stop all' from Control — the block that ends every running script. Notice the difference: (=) ASKS a question — 'is lives 0?' — while 'set' MAKES it that number. Asking never changes the number.

steps.title: Make it yours
steps.text: New costumes for the apple and bowl, new backdrop, new sounds — from the Scratch libraries or draw your own. Re-skin everything; the brief only cares that it WORKS.

blueprint.imgAlt: The finished Catch It if/else: touching Bowl scores and plays pop, else lives drops and game over fires at zero
blueprint.imgCaption: The finished landing check — yours should read like this.

criteria.name: The catch scores
criteria.test: Click the green flag. Catch ONE apple — just one — and watch the score before and after.
criteria.ask: What did the score actually do?

outcomes.t: Up by exactly 1, exactly when I caught it.
It kept climbing on its own, without me catching anything.
outcomes.fix: Your change-score block is loose inside the fall loop, so it fires every tick. It must live inside the if's TOP mouth — points only exist when 'touching Bowl?' is true.
outcomes.mech: Drag change score by 1 INTO the top mouth of the if/else, right under the touching Bowl condition.

outcomes.t: Nothing — the score never moved.
outcomes.fix: Either the if/else isn't inside the forever (so it ran once, ages ago), or its condition isn't checking the Bowl. Both mean the catch is invisible to your code.
outcomes.mech: Check the if/else sits AFTER the fall loop, INSIDE the forever — and click its condition dropdown: it must say Bowl.

outcomes.t: The score went up even when I MISSED.
outcomes.fix: Scoring is happening outside the choice. If change score sits outside the if/else, every apple pays out, caught or dropped — selection means the game must CHOOSE.
outcomes.mech: Move change score by 1 inside the if's top mouth so only a real catch counts.

criteria.name: A miss costs a life
criteria.test: Click the green flag. DODGE on purpose: steer the bowl away from each apple and let THREE miss, watching the lives counter.

outcomes.t: Down by exactly 1 per dodge — 3, 2, 1 — and the score never moved.
Lives never moved at all.
outcomes.fix: Nothing is handling the miss. That's exactly what ELSE is for: the bottom mouth runs when the answer to 'touching Bowl?' is no. Also check the flag sets lives to 3 — a variable that's never set can't count down.
outcomes.mech: Drag change lives by -1 into the BOTTOM mouth (else). Check set lives to 3 sits at the flag.

outcomes.t: I lost a life even when I CAUGHT the apple.
outcomes.fix: Your lives block is running on both branches — it's sitting outside the else, or after the whole if/else. If/else picks exactly ONE mouth: catch = top, miss = bottom.
outcomes.mech: Move change lives by -1 so it sits INSIDE the else mouth and nowhere else.

outcomes.t: Lives went UP, or dropped by more than 1 at a time.
outcomes.fix: The number on the block is wrong. A miss costs exactly one life: change lives by -1 — minus one, once, in the else mouth.
outcomes.mech: Click the number in change lives by and retype -1.

outcomes.t: Lives behaved — but the SCORE also changed while I was dodging.
outcomes.fix: That's not a lives bug — your scoring is loose. If change score sits outside the if/else, every apple pays out, dodged or not. Check 1's fix is your fix.
outcomes.mech: Move change score by 1 INSIDE the if's top mouth (see QA check 1), then run this dodge test again.

criteria.name: One fall, one outcome
criteria.test: Catch one apple, then deliberately miss one — watching BOTH counters each time.
criteria.ask: For a single apple, what happened?

outcomes.t: Exactly one thing each time: a catch moved only the score, a miss moved only lives.
One apple changed BOTH — score up AND a life gone.
outcomes.fix: One of your blocks has escaped the if/else, so it runs no matter which branch fires. The whole point of selection: one situation, one branch, never both.
outcomes.mech: Both blocks live INSIDE the if/else — score in the top mouth, lives in the bottom. Nothing score-ish after it.

outcomes.t: Sometimes an apple fell and NOTHING changed.
outcomes.fix: Your if/else probably runs once instead of every fall — it has slipped outside the forever loop. Every single apple needs its own landing check.
outcomes.mech: Drag the whole if/else INSIDE the forever, straight after the fall loop.

criteria.name: Game over means over
criteria.test: Lose all 3 lives on purpose. Then try to keep playing.
criteria.ask: At zero lives, what did the game do?

outcomes.t: Said 'Game over!' and froze — no more falling, no more scoring.
It said game over… but apples kept falling and scoring.
outcomes.fix: 'Say' isn't 'stop'. After the message the game needs 'stop all' — the block that ends every running script.
outcomes.mech: Inside if lives = 0, after the say block: add 'stop all' from Control.

outcomes.t: Nothing happened — lives just kept going: -1, -2, -3…
outcomes.fix: Nothing is checking lives. The check belongs right where a life is lost: inside the else, straight after change lives by -1 — the only moment lives can hit zero.
outcomes.mech: Drag an if into the else under change lives by -1. Condition: Operators (=) with lives and 0.

outcomes.t: The game ended too early, before my lives ran out.
outcomes.fix: Either lives never started at 3, or the condition isn't asking for exactly 0. Set lives to 3 at the flag; the check reads lives = 0.
outcomes.mech: Check the flag script sets lives to 3, and the if condition reads lives = 0 exactly.

stretch.title: The second variable
stretch.text: Real games get harder as you go. Add a SECOND variable and make it matter: a timer counting down, a level that speeds the fall every 5 points, a streak that doubles the next catch. Your studio, your call — then test it like everything else.
stretch.placeholder: I added a ... variable that ... — tested and working.

maze.name: Maze Escape
maze.noteWhere: Click the Door in the sprite list — the STUDIO NOTE is stuck to its code.

blueprint.title: The Maze Escape blueprint
blueprint.intro: Four moves. The kit already punishes wall-touches — READ that script first (it's a working if, your best evidence). The STUDIO NOTE on the Door marks where your if/else lands.

steps.title: Make the stars variable
steps.text: Variables → Make a Variable → 'stars', for all sprites. Its counter appears on stage — leave the tick on so players can see it climb.

steps.title: Set it at the flag
steps.text: On the Beetle's when-flag script, after point in direction: set stars to 0. Variables remember between games — no reset, no fresh start.

steps.title: Count on ALL THREE stars
steps.text: Open Star1: its pickup script already plays the sound and hides — drop change stars by 1 between them. Now do the same on Star2 and Star3. Every sprite owns its scripts (the Lesson 4 rule): one edited star leaves two that still can't count.

steps.title: The door's if/else — the big one
steps.text: Open the Door. The STUDIO NOTE points at the gap between 'wait until touching Beetle' and 'wait until NOT touching Beetle'. Put an if/else there, with Operators' (=) asking stars = 3. Top mouth: switch costume to door-open, say 'You escaped!' for 2 seconds, then 'stop all'. Else: say 'Locked! Collect all 3 stars.' for 2 seconds. Notice the difference: (=) ASKS a question — 'is stars 3?' — while 'set' MAKES it so. Asking never changes the number.

steps.title: Make it yours
steps.text: Re-skin the beetle, the stars, the backdrop — haunted house? space station? You can even redraw the Maze sprite's walls in the paint editor (keep them solid — the bounce needs something to touch).

blueprint.imgAlt: The finished Door if/else: stars = 3 opens the door and stops the game, else the door stays locked
blueprint.imgCaption: The finished door check — yours should read like this.

criteria.name: Every star counts
criteria.test: Click the green flag. Collect all three stars, watching the stars counter after each one.

outcomes.t: It went 0, then 1, then 2, then 3 — one for each star.
Stars vanished, but the counter stayed on 0.
outcomes.fix: The pickups still aren't counting. Each star needs change stars by 1 inside its touching-Beetle if — and check the counter exists: did you make the variable and set it to 0 at the flag?
outcomes.mech: Open each Star sprite: drag change stars by 1 into the if, between the sound and the hide.

outcomes.t: ONE star counted — the other two didn't.
outcomes.fix: You've edited one star and left its siblings unfinished. Every sprite owns its own scripts (the Lesson 4 rule) — the block you added to Star1 doesn't exist on Star2 or Star3 until you put it there.
outcomes.mech: Click Star2 in the sprite list, add change stars by 1 to its if. Repeat for Star3.

outcomes.t: The counter jumped past 3, or double-counted a star.
outcomes.fix: Either stars never resets (set stars to 0 at the flag) or a star counts more than once — the hide must come straight after the count, so a collected star can't keep counting.
outcomes.mech: Check the Beetle's flag script sets stars to 0. Then check each star's script runs in this order: play the sound, change stars by 1, then hide.

criteria.name: The door refuses early guests
criteria.test: Fresh green flag. Go STRAIGHT to the door with zero stars and touch it.

outcomes.t: Called me out — 'Locked! Collect all 3 stars.' — and the game carried on.
Nothing. The door ignored me completely.
outcomes.fix: The doorbell rings, but nobody answers: your if/else isn't in the door's script yet. The kit only SENSES the beetle — deciding what to do about it is your job.
outcomes.mech: Open the Door sprite: the if/else goes in the gap between the two wait-until blocks (the STUDIO NOTE marks it).

outcomes.t: It let me escape with ZERO stars!
outcomes.fix: The branches are swapped or the condition is wrong. 'You escaped!' belongs in the TOP mouth — the branch that runs when stars = 3 is TRUE. Else is the door saying no.
outcomes.mech: Check the condition reads stars = 3, with 'You escaped!' in the top mouth and 'Locked!' in the else.

criteria.name: Three stars open the door
criteria.test: Collect all three stars, then walk to the door and touch it.

outcomes.t: It went green, said 'You escaped!' — and the game stopped for good.
Still locked, even with all 3 stars collected.
outcomes.fix: The condition can't see your stars. It must compare the round orange stars VARIABLE with 3 — a typed word 'stars' is just text. And if QA check 1 isn't green yet, the counter may never have reached 3 at all.
outcomes.mech: In the (=) block: left side is the orange stars oval dragged from Variables, right side is 3.

outcomes.t: It said 'You escaped!' but the game kept running behind the message.
outcomes.fix: An escape should end the run — that's the END part of the brief. After the say, the top mouth needs 'stop all' — the block that ends every running script.
outcomes.mech: Add 'stop all' from Control, right after 'You escaped!' inside the top mouth.

criteria.name: The walls still bite
criteria.test: After ALL your changes: run into a wall on purpose. Twice.

outcomes.t: Bounced me back to the start, both times. My edits broke nothing.
I walked straight through a wall like a ghost.
outcomes.fix: Somewhere in the sprint, the wall rule got broken — a studio re-tests EVERYTHING before shipping, because new code can break old code. Restore the Beetle's wall script: it's a working if you can read.
outcomes.mech: The Beetle's second flag script must read: forever, and inside it, if touching Maze then go to x -165 y 0.

outcomes.t: The wall bounced me somewhere strange, not the start.
outcomes.fix: The go-to inside the wall rule has drifted. It should send the beetle to the exact start position — the same x and y the flag script uses.
outcomes.mech: Compare the wall rule's go-to with the flag script's go-to: both read x -165, y 0.

stretch.title: The countdown
stretch.text: Escape rooms have clocks. Add a SECOND variable: a timer ticking down from 60 (escape before zero!), or a moves counter for a par score. Make it change something real — then test it like everything else.
stretch.placeholder: I added a ... variable that ... — tested and working.

quiz.name: Quiz Master
quiz.noteWhere: Click the True Tile in the sprite list — the STUDIO NOTE is stuck to its code, and a matching note sits on the False Tile.

blueprint.title: The Quiz Master blueprint
blueprint.intro: Five moves — then the best bit: the questions become YOURS. The STUDIO NOTE on each tile marks where your if/else lands. The kit already owns two variables, q and answer — they are the host's wiring, so leave them alone and do not rebuild them. The one NEW variable your studio makes is the score. (When you write your own questions in the final step, you will set each question's answer to true or false — step 6 shows you how.)

steps.title: Make the score
steps.text: Variables → Make a Variable → 'score', for all sprites. Its counter appears on stage — the audience needs to see it, so leave the tick on.

steps.title: Set it at the flag
steps.text: On the host's when-flag script, before question 1: set score to 0. Variables remember between games — skip this and every new contestant inherits the last one's points.

steps.title: The True tile's if/else — the big one
steps.text: Open the True Tile. Your if/else REPLACES the grey say block — the STUDIO NOTE marks it. The condition asks: answer = true. In the top mouth: say 'Correct!' for 1 second, then change score by 1. In the else mouth: say 'Not this time!' for 1 second. Keep 'broadcast next' underneath — it asks for the next question. Notice the difference: (=) ASKS a question — 'is the answer true?' — while 'set' MAKES it so. Asking never changes anything.

steps.title: Now the False tile
steps.text: Same job, one twist: this tile is right when the answer is FALSE — its condition reads answer = false. Praise and point in the top mouth, 'Not this time!' in the else, broadcast next stays at the bottom.

steps.title: The finale
steps.text: In the host's final message, swap the plain say for Operators' join: first slot 'That's the quiz! You scored ', second slot the orange score variable. Now the show ends with YOUR contestant's number in lights.

steps.title: Write YOUR quiz
steps.text: Rewrite the three questions in the host's scripts on any topic you like — and set each question's answer to true or false to match. Wrong answer settings are the quizmaster's own bug: QA will find it.

blueprint.imgAlt: The finished True Tile if/else: answer = true scores and praises, else Not this time
blueprint.imgCaption: The finished tile check — yours should read like this.

criteria.name: Right answers score
criteria.test: Click the green flag. Answer question 1 CORRECTLY and watch the score.

outcomes.t: 'Correct!' — and the score climbed by exactly 1.
It said 'Correct!' but the score never moved.
outcomes.fix: The praise runs but the points don't — change score by 1 must sit in the SAME top mouth as the 'Correct!' say. If it's below the if/else, it never met the choice.
outcomes.mech: Drag change score by 1 into the if's top mouth, next to say 'Correct!'.

outcomes.t: Nothing at all — no reply, no point.
outcomes.fix: The tile still can't check answers — the if/else hasn't replaced the grey say block yet, or the whole script lost its broadcast. The tile needs: check the answer, respond, THEN broadcast next.
outcomes.mech: Open the tile: if/else replaces the grey say (STUDIO NOTE marks it); broadcast next stays at the bottom.

outcomes.t: It said 'Not this time!' to a RIGHT answer.
outcomes.fix: The tile is checking the wrong word. The True tile asks answer = true — a misspelling ('ture'), a stray space, or the False tile's word in the True tile breaks the match every time.
outcomes.mech: Click the (=) block's text slot and retype: true — no stray spaces or extra characters.

criteria.name: Wrong answers don't
criteria.test: Fresh green flag. Answer question 1 WRONGLY on purpose. Watch the score AND what happens next.

outcomes.t: 'Not this time!' — no point, and the next question arrived anyway.
A wrong answer still scored a point!
outcomes.fix: Points are leaking through the choice. If change score sits outside the if/else — or in the else mouth — every click pays out. Points live ONLY in the top mouth. Check BOTH tiles.
outcomes.mech: On each tile: change score by 1 belongs inside the if's TOP mouth, nowhere else.

outcomes.t: The quiz got stuck — no reply ever came, or no next question.
outcomes.fix: The broadcast has gone missing. Right or wrong, the tile must still ask for the next question — 'broadcast next' runs AFTER the if/else, every click.
outcomes.mech: Put broadcast next back at the bottom of the tile's click script, below the if/else.

criteria.name: The score keeps up
criteria.test: Play the whole quiz. Watch the score display on stage the entire time.

outcomes.t: On stage the whole time — climbing on rights, holding still on wrongs.
There's no score on the stage at all.
outcomes.fix: The variable exists, but it's invisible — and a quiz show without a scoreboard is just a chat. The checkbox beside the variable puts it on stage.
outcomes.mech: In the Variables group, tick the checkbox beside score.

outcomes.t: It started from last game's total instead of 0.
outcomes.fix: Variables remember! Without 'set score to 0' at the flag, every new game starts with the last game's points still in the box — the sneakiest bug in the studio.
outcomes.mech: Add set score to 0 to the host's when-flag script, before question 1.

criteria.name: A proper finale
criteria.test: Answer all three questions, then watch what happens after question 3 — and try one extra click.

outcomes.t: The host announced my actual score — and late clicks couldn't change it.
It ended with a plain 'That's the quiz!' — no score in sight.
outcomes.fix: The finale hasn't been upgraded. The join block glues your words and the live score into one announcement — that's the difference between an ending and a FINALE.
outcomes.mech: Operators → join. Slot 1: 'That's the quiz! You scored '. Slot 2: the orange score variable. Drop the join into the final say.

outcomes.t: It announced 'You scored score' — the word, not the number!
outcomes.fix: The word 'score' got typed where the VARIABLE should sit. The typed word is just text; the orange oval from Variables is the live number.
outcomes.mech: Drag the round orange score block into join's second slot, replacing the typed word.

stretch.title: The bonus round
stretch.text: Add a SECOND variable and raise the stakes: a streak that doubles the next point after two rights in a row, or lives — two wrong answers and the show ends early. Test it like everything else.
stretch.placeholder: I added a ... variable that ... — tested and working.

config.intro: The doors are open across the studio floor. Half the room EXHIBITS — shows their game at their own desk — while the other half TOURS the room playing them. Then you swap. You are about to give, and get, your first real reviews. Every review follows the Reviewer's Code, and every review is signed. You have TWO PRESS PASSES to spend — each pass is one signed review you write about another studio's game.

rules: KIND — you're reviewing the game, never the maker. Reviews build studios up.
SPECIFIC — name the exact moment. 'The wasabi near the end got me twice' beats 'it's good' every time.
HELPFUL — your 'I wonder' should hand the studio a real idea for version 2.
code.badExample: "it was good i liked it" — kind, but it tells the studio nothing.
code.goodExample: "I like how the lives counter makes every drop feel risky — I wonder what a golden apple worth 3 points would add."

rounds.note: Two rounds — your teacher calls the swap.
rounds.exhibitTip: Have your game running FULL SCREEN in Scratch, with this marquee page beside it. Welcome your players, show them the controls, and watch your reviews land below. Still in beta? Exhibit anyway — reviews are written about what is there.

config.deskNote: Play it at their desk first — and as you play, ask like a reviewer: does it REACT? TRACK? END? Then write your review: kind, specific, helpful.

config.title: Ship your game
config.intro: Your game is real now — and a real game must not live and die on one classroom machine. This is the same save-to-Drive routine as every build this term: three steps, about a minute. Then your game follows your login home — any school computer, any time.

steps.title: Save your game
steps.text: In Scratch, open the File menu and choose 'Save to your computer'. The .sb3 lands in Downloads — that file IS your game.

steps.title: Put it in your Drive
steps.text: Open drive.google.com, click into School, then DT Work, and drag the .sb3 in. The same folder as everything you have saved this term.

steps.title: Run the check
steps.text: The website looks in your Drive for a freshly-saved .sb3. Your game now follows your login home.

config.help: Shipping your game takes three steps. First, save the .sb3 from Scratch: open the File menu and choose 'Save to your computer'. Then drag that file into your Google Drive, into School, then DT Work. Last, press Check my Drive. The website really does look in your Drive, the same check as every build this term.

config.intro: Two questions about today before you go — and these ARE marked: your teacher sees your answers. Think like a designer AND a tester.

items.stem: In an if/else block, what happens when the condition turns out to be FALSE?
options: The blocks in the ELSE mouth run
Both sets of blocks run, one after the other
Scratch stops the script with an error

items.stem: A studio spent the whole sprint on gorgeous costumes and a stunning backdrop — but never added the variable their brief required. The game LOOKS incredible. Have they met the brief?
options: Yes — it looks finished, so it is finished
Yes — great decoration can stand in for one missing check
No — the brief tests what the game DOES, and looks can't pass a QA test
No — because changing costumes isn't allowed

config.help: Two marked questions, answered on your own. You find out how you did at the end, after the last screen.

config.intro: Last job of the night. You get five real blocks, and the sentence below describes one clean scoring loop — the exact pattern your game shipped with. Click the blocks into the order the sentence describes.

item.prompt: The score starts at zero. Every time the sprite touches the ball, the score goes up by one; otherwise the game just takes a breath — and keeps checking, forever.
blocks: if <touching Ball?> then → change score by 1

config.help: Click blocks from the tray into your program, in the order the sentence describes. Check when you're sure — you'll be shown the working order if it's off.
config.doneText: Correct — that program does exactly what the card asked.
